creative.body:
If your oncology chart says "no estrogen" and your last appointment ended with someone suggesting coconut oil, this is for you. There is a non-hormonal first-line option buried in the ASCO clinical guidelines that almost no one is telling cancer survivors about.

I know, because I had to find it on my own, at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday, 3 years after my diagnosis, with my husband asleep in the next room and a Reddit tab open on my laptop. I am a breast cancer survivor. ER-positive, PR-positive, stage 1. 3 years out.

Lumpectomy, 6 weeks of radiation, 2 years of tamoxifen, and now letrozole, which my oncologist informed me, in a sentence she had clearly delivered hundreds of times before, would "drop my estrogen to undetectable."

She said it the way you read a weather report. She did not mention what undetectable estrogen would do to my marriage.

The cancer is the easy part. The cancer has a treatment plan, a finish line, a scan that says no evidence of disease.

Survivorship has none of those.

Survivorship is what happens when the tumor is gone but the medication is forever, and the medication takes one specific thing from you that nobody, not your oncologist, not your PA, not the 8 pamphlets you got in the chemo lounge, will fully explain.

They take your estrogen. They do not tell you what comes with that. What comes with that is a body that no longer knows itself. I started flinching when my husband reached for me. Sex, when we attempted it, felt like sandpaper rubbing over an open wound.

I bled afterward. I bled sometimes after walking. I stopped initiating. Then I stopped responding. Then he stopped reaching. 27 years of marriage and we suddenly had this thing between us that neither of us could name without crying. So I went to my oncologist. I told her, with my voice shaking, that sex was painful.

She nodded. She told me I could "try Replens." When I asked about anything else, she explained, kindly, professionally, regretfully, that estrogen was off the table for me. ER-positive cancer means the cancer feeds on estrogen. The whole point of letrozole is to make sure there is no estrogen anywhere for a cancer cell to find.

So the only thing the medical system has built for women like me, over the last 50 years, is the one thing I cannot have. I want to say something here that I could not say out loud for a long time.

The "try Replens" line is not a treatment plan. It is the polite version of standard of care. It is what a kind oncologist says to a survivor at the end of a 15-minute appointment when there is nothing on the formulary she is allowed to give you and the next patient is in the waiting room.

It is the system telling you, in the gentlest possible voice, that the part of survivorship the medication is going to take from you is not the system's department. The cancer was the department. You graduated. The dryness, the burning, the marriage, those are yours now. Good luck.

Coconut oil is the polite version of nothing. Replens is the polite version of nothing. They are surface answers to a tissue problem. They are what gets handed to you when nothing else has been built. At my next visit I told my oncologist plainly that none of it was working. She was kind. She always is.

She said something I had not heard her say before. She said, "We can revisit vaginal estrogen at year 5 if you are still NED and still struggling."

Year 5. I am 3 years out. Year 5 was 2 more years away. I drove home from that appointment and pulled into my own driveway and put the car in park. I sat there for 22 minutes. I know it was 22 minutes because I watched the dashboard clock change. My husband's truck was already in the driveway. He had no idea I was sitting in the car.

I was doing the math. 2 more years of flinching when he reached for me. 2 more years of the woman I used to be getting a little farther away each month. 2 more years of waiting for permission from a system that had told me, kindly and professionally, that the part of survivorship the medication takes was not its department.

I made a decision in the car with the engine off. I was not going to wait 2 more years. I went inside, kissed my husband, made dinner, washed the dishes, and after he went to bed I opened my laptop.

That is the night I started actually researching. Here is what I learned, in plain English, after 30 hours of reading. The reason sex hurts after estrogen drops is not that you are not lubricated enough. The tissue itself actually changes.

The walls thin. The blood supply shrinks. And the good bacteria that used to live there, the ones that evolved alongside estrogen for 2 million years, start dying off because their food source is gone. Estrogen used to keep glycogen levels high. Glycogen is what those good bacteria eat.

No estrogen, no glycogen, no bacteria, no protection. So you end up with a triple problem. Tissue that is thinner and more fragile. A bacterial environment that has collapsed. And no fuel system to support either one. Lube does not fix any of those 3 things. Lube is paint on a wall that is falling down.

Replens does a little better than lube, it sticks around longer and adds moisture, but it does not restore the bacteria, and it does not feed the bacteria, and it does not rebuild the tissue. Replens is one piece of a 4-piece puzzle. It has been one piece of a 4-piece puzzle for 40 years. It is not getting upgraded.

Here is the part that changed everything for me. The American Society of Clinical Oncology, the people who actually write the guidelines for cancer doctors, published a clinical practice guideline in 2018 about cancer survivors and sexual health. It says, in plain language, that non-hormonal vaginal moisturizers are recommended as first-line therapy for cancer survivors with vaginal symptoms. The 2023 NCCN survivorship guideline says the same thing.

First-line. That is the medical term for this is what you should try first. Nobody had ever offered me a first-line treatment. They had offered me Replens. Replens is a non-hormonal moisturizer, technically, but it does only one of the 4 things my body needs.

I started looking for something that did all 4. Hydrate the tissue. Restore the bacteria. Feed the bacteria. Sustain the work over time. I want to take a moment on the natural-means-safe trap. I found a lot of "natural" options. Most of them were phytoestrogens. Pueraria mirifica. Red clover. Black cohosh.

My oncologist wrote back in 14 minutes. No phytoestrogens. That ruled out probably 70 percent of what gets marketed to menopausal women, and almost all of it was being sold to me as natural. The word natural is doing a lot of work in that aisle, and almost none of it is the work survivors need it to do.

Phytoestrogens are plant compounds that mimic estradiol at the receptor. For a woman whose entire medication regimen is designed to make sure no molecule that looks like estrogen reaches a cancer cell, that mimicry is the exact thing you are paying letrozole to prevent.

Natural is not a safety claim for us. The only safety claim that matters is the ingredient panel, read line by line, and the molecule, verified by your oncology team. I tried plain hyaluronic-acid suppositories. They were better than Replens. But they only did the hydration part. The bacteria part was still missing.

Somewhere in those weeks I called the cancer center where I had been treated and asked whether they had a survivorship social worker on staff. They did. Real role, licensed clinical social worker, embedded in the oncology team. Her job is to follow survivors after the active treatment ends.

We talked on the phone for almost an hour. She told me, without hedging, that 80% of the survivors who come through her office have stopped having sex by year 2.

She said nobody on the medical chart asks them about it. The chart tracks tumor markers and bone density and lipid panels.

There is no field for whether the marriage is still a marriage.

She said she had stopped being shocked by the number. What shocked her was that the survivors keep apologizing for bringing it up.

I went back to my reading. There was one finding I read 3 times to make sure I had it right. In the Crandall 2018 analysis of the WHI data, low-dose vaginal estrogen did not increase recurrence risk in non-AI survivors.

But for women on aromatase inhibitors specifically, the data was excluded because the absorption math was unresolved. Meaning, the women whose situation is hardest are also the women the data is silent on. I sat with that for a long time. I am one of those women.

There is no published trial that tells my oncologist whether the cream is safe for me. That is why she wants to wait until year 5. The silence in the data is the entire reason for the wait. And then I finally found something called Avelle.

It is a suppository, so it stays where it is needed instead of ending up on your underwear like creams do. It has hyaluronic acid that holds 1,000 times its weight in water for deep moisture, plus healthy bacteria, lactobacillus lactis, and the food the bacteria need to actually survive down there, glycogen, plus a prebiotic fiber, polydextrose, that keeps the colony fed between applications.

Hydrate. Balance. Feed. Sustain.

4 layers, in one suppository, doing the 4 jobs the ASCO guideline says first-line therapy is supposed to do. No estrogen. No phytoestrogens. No DHEA. No hormone analogs. No parabens. No phthalates. The order page said it had been reviewed by oncologists, and the panel read like it had been. There was nothing on it an oncology team could object to.

I screenshotted it and emailed it to my oncologist's PA. She wrote back the next day with the language survivors learn to wait for. No objection.

That was the email I had been waiting 3 years to receive.

I am not going to make a miracle claim. I am 58 and I am on letrozole and I will be on letrozole for 2 more years. There is no product that makes that go away. But after about 3 weeks of using Avelle every other night, I noticed I was not tensing when my husband walked into the bedroom.

After about 6 weeks, I initiated for the first time in 2 years. After about 3 months, the tearing stopped. The bleeding stopped. The "is tonight worth it" math stopped, because the answer was simply yes. There are 2 paths in front of you tonight.

The first path is to accept the second-class prescription. Keep using Replens. Keep being told that survival is enough and that wanting your body and your marriage back is asking for something the medical system has not built for you.

The medication is forever. The waiting, on this path, is also forever. The second path is to print the handout. Bring it to your appointment. Read it with your oncology team. Get the no-objection. Try the first-line non-hormonal the modern guideline endorses, the one that does the 4 jobs the cream used to do, without the molecule your medication is designed to suppress.

There is no third path where Replens starts working better. There is no third path where coconut oil restores a bacterial colony. There is no third path where the medication ends early. The letrozole is forever, the tamoxifen is forever, the no-estrogen rule is forever, and the only thing in that sentence you can move is the waiting.

The risk is not the suppository.

The risk is the months you keep waiting on a path that does not lead anywhere, while your tissue continues to thin and your bacterial environment continues to collapse and the distance between you and your husband continues to grow into something neither of you can name.

You are allowed to want more than lucky. Survival is the floor. It is not the ceiling. The medication is forever. The waiting does not have to be. When I went to order, I saw they had a 90-day money-back guarantee. I read it twice.

I have been on the letrozole side of the chart for almost 3 years, and in those 3 years I have not seen a single pharmaceutical company put that promise on the page. The letrozole did not come with a refund offer. The Replens did not. The hyaluronic acid suppositories I had tried before this did not.

The first product to say in writing that if it did not work in my body I could send it back, was a small company a survivor on Reddit had mentioned at almost midnight on a Tuesday. My daughter is the one who finally said it out loud when I was second-guessing the order. "Mom. 90 days. They are taking the risk for you. What are you waiting for."

She was right. I had been waiting 3 years for someone to take the risk for me, and a company I had never heard of was the first one to do it. I had read enough by then to understand why they made the batches small.

Lactobacillus lactis is a live culture, and the glycogen substrate it feeds on has a defined shelf-active window once the suppository is formed. They batch-produce because they will not ship a bottle whose colony has aged out of viability sitting in a warehouse.

The trade-off is that they sell out for a few weeks at a stretch. If they are in stock the night you read this, that is the night to order. Waiting until next week is how you end up on a list for the next batch instead of starting your 90 days now.

The chart says no estrogen. The chart will say no estrogen for 2 more years, or 5, or forever. The chart is not changing. The only line in that sentence you can move is the waiting. The handout in your hand at the next appointment is how you move it. The "no objection" email from a PA is how my 3 years of waiting ended in one afternoon.
creative.title: If Your Chart Says "No Estrogen," There Is A First-Line Option Nobody Told You About
